name: Pinotage

lines.s10: Pinotage was born in South Africa: a dark, smoky red with black plum, mulberry and a firm grip made for the grill.
lines.s20: Pinotage was bred at the Cape in 1925, a crossing of Pinot Noir and Cinsault. It tastes little like either: black plum, mulberry and wood smoke on a full, firm frame, a natural red for grilled meat.
lines.s45: Pinotage belongs to South Africa: it was bred at Stellenbosch in 1925, and few other countries grow it at all. It makes a dark, full red that tastes of black plum, mulberry and wood smoke, with firm tannin and a warm finish. The classic style is aged in oak barrels and built to keep, and a popular modern one uses heavily toasted oak to give a clear taste of coffee and chocolate. It belongs beside a fire: pour it with grilled lamb, barbecued ribs or smoked sausage. Ask where the name comes from and you have its parents: Pinot Noir, and Cinsault, which the Cape used to call Hermitage.
lines.sale: Pinotage is the taste of one place: South Africa bred it, and its smoky black plum is the flavour of the Cape. It wants anything off the grill, and lamb above all.

glass.lead: Black plum, mulberry and blackberry under wood smoke and a sweet edge of tar, full bodied, with firm tannin.

ladder.where: Walker Bay and the Hemel-en-Aarde, by the cold sea
Paarl, and Bottelary and the warm valley floors of Stellenbosch

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium, tannin medium plus to high, alcohol medium plus to high, body medium to full.

home.home: South Africa, and above all Stellenbosch, where it was bred in 1925. Old bush vines on granite and shale give the dark, smoky classic, fermented in open vats and aged in oak barrels. Heavily toasted oak makes the coffee style, cooler coastal sites a lighter, red cherry one, and it anchors the Cape Blend.
home.abroad: It has barely left the Cape. New Zealand, California, Israel and Brazil each grow a little, and a bottle from any of them is a rarity on a list.

service.temp: 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; a lighter, unoaked one a little cooler.
service.glass: A Bordeaux glass for the dark, oaked wines; a Burgundy bowl suits the lighter style.
service.decant: Consider it for a young, firm bottle, after tasting a sample.
service.age: Three to ten years; the firm old vine wines of Stellenbosch keep longer.

with.dish: Lamb chops or sausage off the grill
with.why: smoke in the wine meets smoke from the fire
ripe plum takes a sweet, smoky glaze
firm tannin and black plum suit lean, rich meat

with.dish: Bobotie or a mild, fragrant curry
with.why: the Cape's own table, ripe fruit against gentle spice

labels.means: A red blend built on Pinotage, generally 30 to 70 per cent of it; a trade term, not a law.
A low vine grown without wires, often old and unirrigated, giving a small crop of concentrated fruit.
A style, not a place: heavily toasted oak gives a plain taste of coffee and chocolate.
South Africa's seal of place, in force since 1973; Stellenbosch, Paarl and Swartland are districts under it.

guest.q: Is it a kind of Pinot Noir?
guest.a: Only by birth. Pinot Noir is one parent and Cinsault the other, but Pinotage is darker, fuller and smokier than either, and closer at the table to a Syrah.

guest.q: I had one years ago that smelled of paint and banana. Are they all like that?
guest.a: No. That came from fermenting too hot and too fast. Careful growers now ferment it cooler and press early, and a good one tastes of black plum, mulberry and smoke.

guest.q: Does this one really taste of coffee?
guest.a: It can. Some cellars use heavily toasted oak to bring out coffee and chocolate on purpose. If you would rather taste the fruit, I will point you to a classic one.

compare.tell: Syrah is peppery and meaty, with black olive; Pinotage has no pepper, and shows mulberry, tar and a sweet smoke like rooibos tea.
Zinfandel is jammier and sweeter in fruit, with raisin at the edges and softer tannin; Pinotage is smokier and firmer, with tar.
Cinsault, its parent, is pale, light and perfumed, with strawberry and soft tannin; Pinotage is far darker and fuller, with smoke and a firm grip.

cards.front: Pinotage: who crossed it, where, when, and from which two grapes?
cards.back: Abraham Perold, at Stellenbosch, in 1925, from Pinot Noir and Cinsault, which the Cape then called Hermitage: hence the name. The name first appeared on a label in 1961.

cards.front: Pinotage: what is a Cape Blend, and is it a legal term?
cards.back: A red blend built on Pinotage, generally 30 to 70 per cent of it, with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot or Shiraz. It is a trade term with no law behind it.

cards.front: Pinotage blind: what gives it away, and which two grapes mislead?
cards.back: Mulberry, black plum, tar and a sweet smoke like rooibos tea, sometimes banana. Syrah is peppery and meaty instead; Zinfandel is jammier, with raisin.

questions.q: A deep ruby red poured blind is full and firm, with black plum, mulberry, tar and a sweet, smoky note like rooibos tea, and no black pepper. Which grape and origin fit?
questions.exp: Mulberry, tar and rooibos smoke with no pepper mark Pinotage. Syrah, the nearest wrong answer, would show cracked black pepper and smoked meat, and Zinfandel is jammier.

questions.q: A guest asks how Pinotage came by its name. Which answer is right?
opts: It crosses Pinot Noir with Cinsault, once called Hermitage
It is Pinot Noir grown in the heat of the Cape
It crosses Pinot Noir with Syrah from the hill of Hermitage
It is an old Cape name for the grape Pinot Meunier
questions.exp: Pinotage is a 1925 crossing of Pinot Noir and Cinsault, which the Cape called Hermitage. The Hermitage in the name is that local alias, not Syrah from the Rhône hill.

questions.q: A guest loved a Pinotage that tasted plainly of coffee and chocolate, and asks how the cellar did it. What do you tell him?
questions.exp: Coffee and chocolate come from heavily toasted oak, used on purpose in this style. A hot, fast fermentation, the nearest wrong answer, gives Pinotage banana and varnish instead.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it, and the home is the New World: South Africa. Abroad is a line only (New Zealand, California, Israel and Brazil, each named in two trade references), since no guest meets a recognised style from any of them.

The two Codex records disagree on structure: the reviewed profile and the dials give acidity medium and tannin medium to high on a medium to full body, the Régionale row body and tannin at their top marks. The entry follows the reviewed profile.

The Codex's Stellenbosch reading says the grape was first sold by a Stellenbosch estate in 1961. The sources read here say the wine of a Stellenbosch estate, of the 1959 vintage, was marketed in 1961 by a merchant firm under its own brand, the first label to carry the name. The entry says only that the name first appeared on a label in 1961.

The national wine body adds that from the 2019 vintage Pinotage should be the major component of a Cape Blend. The entry keeps to the 30 to 70 per cent the Codex and the same page give, and says generally.

The coffee style stands on the Codex's own profile (coffee and mocha in modern styles) and two trade references, which credit heavily toasted oak; the estate and the year they name for the first one are left out, as a producer is never named.

The lighter, red cherry style from cooler sites stands on the Codex's own producer note for Walker Bay and on two trade references. The ladder has no cool rung: the Codex's dials call the grape warm climate.
Left out for want of agreement between sources: the year of the first wine made from the grape (1941, at one of two cellars), and the champion wine trophy of 1959.
No Creole dish is given: the four listed suit it better than any of the seven.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the sites directly. The checker should open the four addresses.

checked.verdict: Sound after four fixes. The crossing at Stellenbosch in 1925, Hermitage, the label of 1961, the Cape Blend at 30 to 70 per cent with no law behind it, the Wine of Origin scheme of 1973 and the cause of the paint and banana note hold; the respelling departed from the Codex records, the sale and the spoken line claimed the grape grew nowhere else, and the ladder set the Codex own cool sites on the moderate rung and a cool corner on the warm one.
changed: say: PIN-oh-tahzh now reads PEE-noh-tahzh, the respelling of the Codex South Africa and Walker Bay records; no source read gives the first syllable as PIN.
lines.s45: could only be South African now reads belongs to South Africa, since the entry own abroad line has New Zealand, California, Israel and Brazil grow a little.
lines.sale: its smoky black plum comes from nowhere else now reads is the flavour of the Cape, for the same reason.

glass.ladder: Walker Bay moves to the cool rung, which the Codex Walker Bay record calls cool maritime, with its Pinotage from cool coastal sites; the sea facing slopes of Stellenbosch leave. The Simonsberg, which the Codex Paarl record calls a cooler corner, and the Swartland, whose Pinotage the Codex calls lighter and whole bunch, leave the warm rung for Paarl, Bottelary and the warm valley floors of Stellenbosch.
open: The paint and banana note: the Codex South Africa record and the research read both put it down to hot, fast fermentation; the research adds stressed vines and the yeast. The guest answer stands.
